body:
Why digital storage needs measurement units

The amount of information stored in a computer may range from a few bits to trillions of bytes. Using individual bits to describe every file or storage device would therefore be inconvenient.

Digital information is measured using bits and bytes, together with larger units such as kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes.

Bits and bytes

The bit is the smallest unit used in the basic binary representation of digital information. The byte is a group of 8 bits.

These units use different symbols:

  • b: bit, written with a lowercase letter.
  • B: byte, written with an uppercase letter.

Because 1 byte contains 8 bits, converting from bytes to bits requires multiplication by 8. Converting from bits to bytes requires division by 8.

Converting bits into bytes

24 bits ÷ 8 = 3 bytes.

Similarly, 5 bytes × 8 = 40 bits.

Decimal storage units

In the internationally standard decimal system, storage prefixes increase by factors of 1,000.

UnitSymbolEquivalent value
ByteB8 bits
KilobytekB1,000 B
MegabyteMB1,000,000 B
GigabyteGB1,000,000,000 B
TerabyteTB1,000,000,000,000 B

Thus, under decimal definitions, 1 MB = 1,000 kB, 1 GB = 1,000 MB and 1 TB = 1,000 GB.

For example, a storage device described as having a capacity of 2 TB has a nominal decimal capacity of 2,000,000,000,000 bytes.

Binary storage units

Computers work with binary information, so quantities based on powers of 2 are also important. A particularly useful quantity is 210 = 1,024.

The internationally standard names for binary multiples use the prefixes kibi, mebi, gibi and tebi.

UnitSymbolEquivalent in bytes
KibibyteKiB1,024 B
MebibyteMiB1,048,576 B
GibibyteGiB1,073,741,824 B
TebibyteTiB1,099,511,627,776 B

Each binary unit is 1,024 times the preceding unit:

  • 1 KiB = 1,024 B.
  • 1 MiB = 1,024 KiB.
  • 1 GiB = 1,024 MiB.
  • 1 TiB = 1,024 GiB.

For example, 2 KiB = 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 bytes.

Why some textbooks use 1 KB = 1,024 bytes

Many introductory computer textbooks traditionally use KB, MB, GB and TB for binary multiples. Under that convention, 1 KB is described as 1,024 bytes, and each larger unit is obtained by multiplying by 1,024.

However, the decimal and binary quantities are not mathematically identical. Standardised terminology distinguishes 1 kB = 1,000 bytes from 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.

When interpreting a storage-capacity statement, identify whether it uses the decimal convention or the binary convention. If an examination question explicitly states a conversion convention, use that convention for the calculation.

Do not treat KB and KiB as universally interchangeable. Older computer textbooks commonly use KB for a binary quantity, while standardised binary terminology uses KiB. The distinction matters in numerical conversions.

Why a 1 TB drive may display about 931 GiB

Storage devices are commonly sold using decimal capacity units. An operating system or utility may report the same number of bytes using binary units.

Since 1 TB equals 1,000,000,000,000 bytes and 1 GiB equals 1,073,741,824 bytes, the same quantity of data can be expressed in either unit:

1,000,000,000,000 ÷ 1,073,741,824 ≈ 931.3 GiB.

Therefore, a drive labelled 1 TB can have a capacity of approximately 931.3 GiB when expressed in binary units. This difference in numerical display does not, by itself, mean storage has been lost.

The usable capacity available for files may also be affected by formatting, file-system information and other reserved space.

Storage size and data-transfer rate

Bits and bytes are also used when describing data-transfer rates. For example, MB/s means megabytes per second, while Mb/s means megabits per second.

Because 1 byte equals 8 bits, 8 megabits correspond to 1 megabyte when both use decimal units. A data-transfer rate of 8 Mb/s is therefore numerically equivalent to 1 MB/s before accounting for communication overhead and other practical limitations.

Storage capacity describes how much data can be held; transfer rate describes how quickly data can be moved.

Prelims focus

  • 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 nibble = 4 bits.
  • Decimal units increase by factors of 1,000.
  • Binary units increase by factors of 1,024.
  • 1 kB = 1,000 B; 1 KiB = 1,024 B.
  • 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 B.
  • Trap: MB means megabyte, while Mb means megabit; uppercase B and lowercase b are not interchangeable.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Definitions of the SI Units: The Binary Prefixes, tables Prefixes for binary multiples and Examples and comparisons with SI prefixes, accessed 14 November 2026; NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Chapter 1, Computer System, §1.3.1, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 14 November 2026; NIOS, Computer Science (330), Lesson 1, Computer Fundamentals, section Measuring Memory, printed p. 13.]

title: Storage Units: Measuring Digital Data From Bit to Terabyte

body:
What is a file format?

A computer stores information in files. A file format specifies how information is organised within a file so that compatible software can interpret it correctly.

For example, a word-processing document contains information organised for text editing, while an image file contains information used to reproduce a picture. Both are ultimately stored as digital bits, but the rules for interpreting their contents are different.

A file's name commonly contains a file extension, usually placed after the final period. The extension helps identify the expected type of file.

For example, in report.pdf, the base file name is report and the extension is .pdf.

The extension helps the operating system select a suitable application, but it does not guarantee that the file's actual contents match the stated format.

Text, document and spreadsheet formats

Different document formats serve different purposes. Some primarily preserve plain text, while others support rich editing, tables, formulas, presentations or a consistent page appearance.

ExtensionFormat or file typeCommon purpose
.txtPlain-text fileStoring text without rich document formatting
.docxWord-processing documentCreating and editing formatted documents
.pdfPortable Document FormatSharing documents with a consistent page appearance
.xlsxSpreadsheet workbookWorking with tabular data, calculations and worksheets
.pptxPresentation filePreparing slide-based presentations
.csvComma-Separated ValuesExchanging simple tabular data
.htmlHyperText Markup Language documentRepresenting the structure of a web page

PDF and DOCX

A PDF is commonly used when a document must be shared or viewed with its intended page layout preserved. An official notice, application form or examination document may be distributed as a PDF.

A DOCX file is commonly used for creating and editing a word-processing document. It supports formatted text and other document elements.

PDF files can also be edited using suitable tools. The main distinction is their usual purpose and document structure, not an absolute rule that PDFs can never be changed.

CSV and XLSX

A CSV file stores tabular data as text records, commonly with commas separating fields. It is useful for exchanging data between compatible applications.

An XLSX file is a spreadsheet workbook format that can preserve worksheets, formulas, formatting and other spreadsheet features.

Therefore, CSV and XLSX are both associated with tabular information, but CSV is a simpler text-based interchange format and does not provide the full workbook features of XLSX.

Image file formats

Digital images can be saved in several formats. The most suitable format depends on factors such as image content, compression, editing needs and compatibility.

ExtensionFormatImportant characteristic
.jpg or .jpegJPEG imageCommon photographic format using lossy compression
.pngPortable Network GraphicsLossless compression; supports transparency
.gifGraphics Interchange FormatSupports simple images and animations
.bmpBitmap imageCommon bitmap-based image format

JPEG and PNG

JPEG commonly uses lossy compression, which reduces file size by discarding some image information. This makes JPEG useful for many photographs where a smaller file is desirable.

PNG uses lossless compression, allowing the encoded image information to be recovered without the compression loss associated with JPEG. PNG is commonly suitable for screenshots, diagrams and images requiring transparency.

Lossless compression does not mean that every PNG file is smaller than a JPEG. For the same image, the file size depends on the image contents, compression method and chosen settings.

GIF

GIF supports simple animations made from multiple image frames. However, a GIF file can also contain a single still image. Therefore, GIF does not always mean animation.

Audio and video formats

Digital audio and video files store information needed to reproduce sound, moving images or both.

ExtensionFile typeTypical use
.mp3Compressed audioMusic and other audio recordings
.wavWaveform audioAudio recordings, often with uncompressed sound
.mp4MPEG-4 multimedia containerVideo, often together with audio
.aviAudio Video InterleaveMultimedia containing video and audio

MP3 is associated with audio compression. MP4 is a multimedia container format commonly used for video and accompanying audio, although it can also contain audio-only content.

A container format organises media streams within a file. The extension alone does not identify every audio or video encoding method used inside that container.

A WAV file often contains uncompressed audio, but the WAV format does not require every possible WAV file to use uncompressed audio.

Compressed archive files

A ZIP file is an archive that can hold multiple files and folders together. ZIP also supports lossless compression, which can reduce the storage required for suitable contents.

A ZIP archive may contain documents, photographs or other files. It is not restricted to any one type of content.

Compression does not always guarantee a large reduction in size. Files that are already heavily compressed may become only slightly smaller when included in a ZIP archive.

Changing an extension does not convert a file

Changing the name of photo.jpg to photo.png does not transform the file's underlying JPEG information into PNG information.

The actual contents remain unchanged. Compatible conversion software must be used when the contents need to be converted into a different file format.

This distinction is important when identifying files. The extension is a useful indication of the intended format, but a file may be misnamed or contain information different from what its extension suggests.

Prelims focus

  • PDF means Portable Document Format.
  • CSV means Comma-Separated Values.
  • DOCX is associated with word processing; XLSX with spreadsheets; PPTX with presentations.
  • JPEG uses lossy compression; PNG uses lossless compression.
  • MP3 is associated with audio; MP4 is a multimedia container commonly used for video.
  • Trap: Changing a file extension does not convert the file's actual format.

[Sources: Microsoft Support, Common file name extensions in Windows, sections Common file name extensions and Open unknown file extensions, accessed 14 November 2026; Mozilla Developer Network, Image file type and format guide, sections Common image file types, GIF, PNG and Choosing an image format, accessed 14 November 2026; Mozilla Developer Network, Media container formats (file types), sections Common container formats and Container selection advice, accessed 14 November 2026.]

body:
Following a file through a computer

Bits, memory, storage devices and file formats describe different aspects of the same digital information. Their relationship becomes easier to understand by examining what happens when a user opens, edits and saves a file.

Consider a document named report.pdf that is stored on an SSD.

  1. The file exists on secondary storage. The SSD preserves the document as digital information even when the computer is switched off.
  2. The user opens the file. A compatible application retrieves the stored information needed to display the document.
  3. Working information is placed in RAM. The computer uses main memory to hold the data and instructions needed during the current task.
  4. The processor uses fast memory. Registers and cache help the CPU work with information required during processing.
  5. The document appears on the screen. The application interprets the PDF information and produces a visual representation for the user.
  6. Changes must be saved when required. If the document is edited, a save operation records the changes in persistent storage. Until saved, some changes may exist only in volatile working memory.

After the computer is shut down, the saved information remains on the SSD, while the ordinary working contents of RAM are lost.

Four distinct questions about digital information

The major concepts in this lesson answer different questions:

  • Binary representation: How is information represented digitally? It is represented through combinations of bits containing 0 and 1.
  • Memory hierarchy: Where is information kept while the CPU is processing it? Registers, cache and RAM provide different levels of fast access.
  • Storage capacity: How much digital information can be held? Bits, bytes, kilobytes, kibibytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes express quantities of data.
  • File format: How should the stored bits be interpreted? Formats such as PDF, JPEG, PNG, MP3 and MP4 specify different kinds of digital content.

These are related but not interchangeable concepts. RAM and SSD describe memory or storage components; GB and TB measure quantities; PDF and JPEG identify formats; and binary describes the underlying representation.

Distinctions that prevent common errors

ConceptsCorrect distinction
Bit and byte1 byte contains 8 bits.
RAM and SSDRAM is volatile working memory; SSD is non-volatile storage.
Cache and storage driveCache reduces access time; a storage drive preserves files.
HDD and SSDHDD uses magnetic rotating platters; SSD uses solid-state storage.
GB and GiBGB is decimal; GiB is binary.
JPEG and PNGJPEG commonly uses lossy compression; PNG uses lossless compression.
MP3 and MP4MP3 is an audio format; MP4 is a multimedia container.
Extension and actual formatThe extension indicates an expected format but does not determine file contents.

One connected view of digital information

A saved file has a format, an amount of data and a storage location. Its contents are represented using bits. When the file is opened, information needed for processing is made available in working memory, and faster memory levels help the processor access selected information efficiently.

The same PDF file could be stored on an HDD, SSD or USB flash drive without changing its PDF format. Similarly, the same storage device can contain documents, photographs, audio files and videos. The device describes where the data are stored, while the format describes how the stored information is organised and interpreted.

Prelims focus

  • Binary digits are the underlying units used to represent digital information.
  • RAM supports active processing; secondary storage retains saved information.
  • Cache improves access to frequently needed information.
  • Storage units measure data quantity, not file type.
  • A file format determines how stored information is organised and interpreted.
  • Trap: A file's storage device, capacity and format describe different properties and should not be confused.

[Sources: NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Chapter 1, Computer System, §§1.1–1.3, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 14 November 2026; NIOS, Computer Science (330), Lesson 1, Computer Fundamentals, §1.6, printed pp. 12–18; NIST, Definitions of the SI Units: The Binary Prefixes, section Examples and comparisons with SI prefixes, accessed 14 November 2026; Microsoft Support, Common file name extensions in Windows, accessed 14 November 2026.]
